Morgan Stanley’s 2027 outlook goes “max overweight” global stocks, saying “With risk assets having cheapened, we embrace risk.” It added to equities in every region:

▪️ U.S. stays overweight; Japan and Europe raised to overweight; EM stays equal weight.
▪️ End-2027 targets: S&P 500 8,700 (+15%), TOPIX 4,800 (+22%), MSCI Europe 3,030 (+15%), MSCI EM 1,760 (+13%).
▪️ Funded by cutting the rest of fixed income, commodities and cash; corporate credit raised to equal weight; likes gold.
▪️ Expects $1.7T of hyperscaler capex in 2027 and $1.8T in 2028, and says AI is broadening to adopters.

Wilson’s new 8,700 target (from 8,000) is 19x his 2028 EPS of $458. His EPS path is $369 / $420 / $458 for 2026–28 (+34% / +14% / +9%).

So the whole target raise has come from earnings. Since May Wilson has lifted his 2027 EPS 11% while cutting the multiple to 19x from about 20.5x. Notably his 14% 2027 growth is still below the 16.2% analysts expect (FactSet).

Note also the bank is calling for the 10-year Treasury rate to fall to 5.05% in 1H27 even with two more Fed rate hikes. The S&P’s forward earnings yield (18.3x per FactSet) is about 5.5%, only about a third of a point over the current 5.14% 10-year. On trailing earnings, stocks now yield 1.31 points less than the 10-year, the widest gap since 2009. 

With Goldman and Barclays also at 8,700 for next year, the debate is whether the earnings show up. Wilson also says says a retest of 7,100–7,300 “could still lie ahead.”

“Our view dating back to late September has been that the correction associated with the mid cycle transition would conclude with the S&P 500 catching down to narrow breadth. That process is now well advanced as the index has approached our established 7,100–7,300 support range,” he said. “While a retest could still lie ahead, the recent correction provides the springboard for the next leg higher toward our new 8,700 base case.”

From @C_Barraud’s packed Monday Morning Brief, @AndreasSteno says “Everything is upside down to the dot com pricing.”

Two of the valuation items in the brief (the second from @MikeZaccardi via @yardeni):

▪️ In March 2000, S&P tech traded at 55x and Cisco at 130x, while Staples sat at 17x. Today, as I mentioned last week, the Nasdaq-100 is at about 18x, the lowest since the Covid crash. Nvidia is at 11x and Micron at 4x, while Walmart and Costco trade at 40x and 42x.
▪️ Consumer Staples’ forward P/E has climbed to 24.2x, the highest since 1999. That’s well above its 5-year (20.8x) and 10-year (20.1x) averages.

Goldman’s thematic desk was already leaning against the move last week. As I noted in that week’s Week Ahead (https://t.co/JZ7uYgRz4o), it liked shorting its Staples basket, which had beaten the S&P 500 by nearly 20% over the prior month. They noted similar metrics:

▪️ S&P Staples’ valuation premium to the index is the highest in more than 10 years.
▪️ The basket’s 2.84% dividend yield is 2.05pp below the 10-year Treasury yield, the 1st percentile of the last 10 years.
▪️ Historically, Staples have lagged over the next three months after similar runs, except in late 2021/early 2022.

Looking at the charts, on Nov 5, $XLP’s one-month lead over $SPY hit +18.4%. Only April and October 2000 and March 2020 were higher. Since 1999 there have been 10 earlier runs of 12% or more, and XLP lagged over the next three months in 6 of them (median −4.5%).

The exceptions: 2000 (twice), late 2008 and 2022. Each came during an S&P 500 bear market that kept grinding lower over the next three months. Being in a bear market wasn’t enough on its own though: the 2001 and March 2020 runs also came during bear markets, and Staples lagged as stocks bounced. So the short is really a bet on a rebound.

Even if it is a 2000 replay, the starting point is very different. Staples went into the dot-com unwind at 17x. They’re going into this one at 24x.

Looking at the seasonality breakdown from @AlmanacTrader, editor of the Stock Trader’s Almanac & Almanac Investor Newsletter, this week we hit the low point of November’s mid-month dip, with the caveat that we haven’t done a very good job of following the seasonal pattern so far this month (more on that in a minute).

In midterm years, Tuesday (day 12) has brought the sharpest drop. The Nasdaq has fallen about 0.8%, the Russell 2000 about 0.7%, the S&P 500 and Russell 1000 about 0.5%, and the DJIA about 0.45%. Hirsch flags the same day for small caps across all years: the Russell 2000 has risen on the 12th trading day just 12 times in the last 42 years, averaging −0.39%. The midterm lines bottom by Wednesday and rebound Thursday and Friday, leaving the week down about 0.15–0.3%.

Friday is also monthly options expiration, which falls in the week before Thanksgiving this year. Hirsch notes the DJIA rose in this week ten straight years from 1993 to 2002 and has been up in 21 of the last 33, but it has been down in seven of the last nine. Expiration day itself has a bullish bias, with the DJIA up 17 of the last 24, though five of the declines have come in the last ten years. The 21-year averages fit that recent record: the week is down, but Friday is up.

From the day-14 low, the strong finish in Hirsch’s pattern takes over, with every index rallying through Thanksgiving week into month-end.

As noted, though, November is lagging the typical seasonal pattern. The S&P 500 is down 0.2% for the month through day 10 (from −2.7% through day 5), and the Nasdaq-100 1.6% (from −4.9%), versus 21-year average gains of roughly 0.7%–1.2% for the major indices by this point (about 1.8%–2.3% in midterm years), again reinforcing that seasonality is just a general guide to how markets have historically performed, certainly not a prediction of how they will actually perform.

The midterm lines bottom by Wednesday and rebound Thursday and Friday, leaving the week down about 0.15–0.3%.

Friday is also monthly options expiration, which falls in the week before Thanksgiving this year. Hirsch notes the DJIA rose in this week ten straight years from 1993 to 2002 and has been up in 21 of the last 33, but it has been down in seven of the last nine. Expiration day itself has a bullish bias, with the DJIA up 17 of the last 24, though five of the declines have come in the last ten years. The 21-year averages fit that recent record: the week is down, but Friday is up.

From the day-14 low, the strong finish in Hirsch’s pattern takes over, with every index rallying through Thanksgiving week into month-end.

As noted, though, November is lagging the typical seasonal pattern. The S&P 500 is down 0.2% for the month through day 10 (from −2.7% through day 5), and the Nasdaq-100 1.6% (from −4.9%), versus 21-year average gains of roughly 0.7%–1.2% for the major indices by this point (about 1.8%–2.3% in midterm years), again reinforcing that seasonality is just a general guide to how markets have historically performed, certainly not a prediction of how they will actually perform.

@C_Barraud's Top Macro Charts of the Week included a link to a ZeroHedge article on a new Goldman Global Strategy Paper that looks into why China’s growth has never seemed to reach shareholders. Goldman’s interesting conclusion? Capital has been too cheap.

The scorecard:
▪️ China has added about $5T of GDP since Covid, but its stocks have trailed global equities by 110 percentage points since 2020.
▪️ From 2020 to 2026, China is the only market in Goldman’s comparison with a negative dollar return (-22%), vs. +137% for the S&P 500 and +75% for the rest of EM.
▪️ EPS has compounded at just 6% a year since 2021, and ROE has fallen for six straight years even as leverage rose.
▪️ Realized index EPS has missed start-of-year consensus nine years in a row.
▪️ Net share issuance has averaged 0.8% of market cap a year, about 15% cumulative EPS dilution.
Goldman says the problem is that China has “probably one of the lowest COCs [costs of capital] among key markets globally”:
▪️ MSCI China (ex-financials) WACC has fallen from 7.5% in 2020 to 5.4%, while the US went the other way, from 4.9% to 6.0%.
▪️ CSI 300 WACC is down from 9.3% to 3.8%, and the broad “All China” universe from 8.1% to 3.2%.

Why is that a problem? When the hurdle rate is 3%, almost any project clears it. That’s why capex intensity keeps climbing while ROE, ROIC and capacity utilization slide.

Goldman names five causes for the low COC: subsidies, regulatory caps on private-sector profits (Common Prosperity, the 3 Red Lines, the Alibaba and Didi crackdowns), a stimulus bias toward supply over households, the property bust and disinflationary tech. The capacity figures show the result: China’s projected 2026–28 capacity equals 167% of global demand in solar modules, 122% in lithium batteries and 102% in air conditioners.

Two things I’d add:
▪️ The cheap money isn’t free; the banks are absorbing it (which is why Chinese bank profitability is at record lows). Chinese bank net interest margins hit a record-low 1.40% in Q1, below the 1.8% regulators consider healthy, with the 1-year LPR held at a record-low 3.0% for 17 straight months through October. Natixis puts listed-company return on capital at about 6%, vs. more than 11% for global peers.
▪️ 2026 looks set to make it ten years of misses. Goldman’s own China team opened the year calling for 14% EPS growth. Per Bloomberg, consensus 2026 estimates for MSCI China were cut more than 4% from the end of March, and Q3 reporters had missed by about 9% on average as of late October.

Goldman is still constructive. It sees trend EPS growth of 6.4% that AI and “Going Global” could lift to 10% a year over the next five years, with anti-involution a distant third. It pairs that with a 12% normal ROE and 10–15% re-rating upside. It says to avoid the property-linked “Depressed Growth” bucket, where profits have collapsed from RMB1.1T in 2020 to RMB150B, until housing stabilizes, possibly not before 2028/29.

Overall, the findings bolster the arguments of those who say the “return to normal” of rates in the US is not a bad thing. The US is the counterexample: its cost of capital rose 1.1 points over 2020–26, and the S&P 500 still returned 137%. Cheap money didn’t make Chinese companies more profitable; it made them less disciplined.

For investors, it seems the investable part of China is the companies that earn more than their cost of capital.

▪️ MSCI China (ex-financials) WACC has fallen from 7.5% in 2020 to 5.4%, while the US went the other way, from 4.9% to 6.0%.
▪️ CSI 300 WACC is down from 9.3% to 3.8%, and the broad “All China” universe from 8.1% to 3.2%.

Why is that a problem? When the hurdle rate is 3%, almost any project clears it. That’s why capex intensity keeps climbing while ROE, ROIC and capacity utilization slide.

Goldman names five causes for the low COC: subsidies, regulatory caps on private-sector profits (Common Prosperity, the 3 Red Lines, the Alibaba and Didi crackdowns), a stimulus bias toward supply over households, the property bust and disinflationary tech. The capacity figures show the result: China’s projected 2026–28 capacity equals 167% of global demand in solar modules, 122% in lithium batteries and 102% in air conditioners.

Two things I’d add:
▪️ The cheap money isn’t free; the banks are absorbing it (which is why Chinese bank profitability is at record lows). Chinese bank net interest margins hit a record-low 1.40% in Q1, below the 1.8% regulators consider healthy, with the 1-year LPR held at a record-low 3.0% for 17 straight months through October. Natixis puts listed-company return on capital at about 6%, vs. more than 11% for global peers.
▪️ 2026 looks set to make it ten years of misses. Goldman’s own China team opened the year calling for 14% EPS growth. Per Bloomberg, consensus 2026 estimates for MSCI China were cut more than 4% from the end of March, and Q3 reporters had missed by about 9% on average as of late October.

Goldman is still constructive. It sees trend EPS growth of 6.4% that AI and “Going Global” could lift to 10% a year over the next five years, with anti-involution a distant third. It pairs that with a 12% normal ROE and 10–15% re-rating upside. It says to avoid the property-linked “Depressed Growth” bucket, where profits have collapsed from RMB1.1T in 2020 to RMB150B, until housing stabilizes, possibly not before 2028/29.

Overall, the findings bolster the arguments of those who say the “return to normal” of rates in the US is not a bad thing. The US is the counterexample: its cost of capital rose 1.1 points over 2020–26, and the S&P 500 still returned 137%. Cheap money didn’t make Chinese companies more profitable; it made them less disciplined.

For investors, it seems the investable part of China is the companies that earn more than their cost of capital.
